messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
Mr. Nguyen was a 68-year-old widowed public defender from a South Eastern Asian background who had experienced profound trauma after witnessing his wife’s sudden and violent death at the hands of an intruder in their home. The incident occurred one evening when he returned home late from court, only to find his beloved wife lying lifeless on the floor, and the door slightly ajar as if it had been left open by the attacker. Since that fateful day, Mr. Nguyen has experienced an array of symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He describes feeling hypervigilant towards people he encounters, constantly scanning them for signs of danger or hostility. This hyper-awareness often leads him to avoid social gatherings and maintain a guarded demeanor in professional settings. His appetite has also changed dramatically; Mr. Nguyen finds himself overeating as a way to cope with the overwhelming emotions that come with recalling his wife’s death. Food serves as a temporary distraction, providing a momentary respite from the grief and fear that lurk just beneath the surface of his daily life. Mr. Nguyen avoids media coverage of similar events out of fear that watching or reading about such incidents would trigger vivid and distressing memories. This has led him to limit his exposure to news programs and movies, which he once enjoyed as a way to unwind after work. In his occupation as a public defender, Mr. Nguyen’s hypervigilance is particularly pronounced when dealing with defendants who remind him of the intruder. He often finds himself on edge during courtroom proceedings, constantly monitoring both the accused and the surrounding environment for any signs of threat or danger. Mr. Nguyen has developed a habit of repeatedly checking that doors and windows in his home are locked, even though he knows rationally that this does not guarantee safety. The constant need to verify these security measures is a source of significant distress, yet he feels compelled to continue the ritual as a way to assuage his fears. He frequently experiences false alarms, reacting as if he were in immediate danger when there is no real threat present. This hyperarousal often manifests during quiet moments at home or while walking alone, where the slightest noise can trigger an intense fight-or-flight response. Mr. Nguyen’s emotions are characterized by a persistent sense of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. He feels deeply responsible for not being there to protect his wife on that fateful evening, and this guilt weighs heavily on him daily. The grief is overwhelming whenever he recalls the fragmented pieces of the traumatic event, with auditory memories of her voice intermingling with the sounds of the assault. These symptoms have taken a significant toll on Mr. Nguyen’s life. His work as a public defender has become more challenging as his ability to remain objective and focused in court has diminished. The hypervigilance and emotional distress have strained his relationships, particularly with colleagues who notice his increasing isolation and distraction at work. What finally brought Mr. Nguyen to seek help was the realization that he could no longer function effectively in his job or maintain any semblance of a normal life without support. He is most afraid of continuing to be haunted by these memories and losing control completely. At the same time, he is hopeful that with the right intervention, he can reclaim some sense of peace and restore meaning to his daily existence.
